questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Fast fashion, why we buy so much, and the backlash
How clothes are made in big factories in Asia
The best places to buy cheap vintage clothes
How to look good in photos on Instagram
questions.why: They discuss buying clothes and wearing them only a few times, and people pledging to stop.

questions.q: What does Neil say about his own clothes?
options: He buys new clothes every single week online
He only buys second-hand clothes from charity shops
He is wearing a shirt he bought seven years ago
He makes his own clothes with a sewing machine
questions.why: He says, “I for one am wearing the same shirt I bought seven years ago.”

questions.q: Which environmental problem of fast fashion is mentioned?
options: Cotton farms use too much land and water
Shops use too much electricity for their lights
Delivery vans cause traffic jams in the cities
Fibres flow into the sea when clothes are washed
questions.why: Neil says fibre fragments are flowing into the sea when clothes are washed.

questions.q: How many times does the average person wear an item of clothing, according to Georgina?
options: Seventy
Seven
Seventeen
Twice
questions.why: She says she's heard the average time someone wears something is just seven.

questions.q: According to Lauren Bravo, why have clothes become cheaper?
options: Production moved to poorer countries; firms compete on price
Clothes are now made from much cheaper, lower-quality materials
Governments have cut taxes on clothes and shoes in the shops
People buy fewer clothes, so shops have had to cut their prices
questions.why: She says production was offshored to developing countries and the industry keeps undercutting competitors.

questions.q: What does Lauren Bravo mean by 'chasing the cheapest needle'?
options: Buying the cheapest sewing kits in the shops
Workers having to sew faster and faster each day
Shops selling clothes at a loss to attract buyers
The industry always seeking the cheapest producer
questions.why: Georgina explains it means always looking for the company which can make clothes cheaper.

questions.q: What does Lauren Bravo blame for people not wanting to be seen in the same outfit twice?
options: Fashion magazines
TV adverts
Social media
Celebrities
questions.why: She says the feeling “really stems from social media”, with people buying outfits for Instagram photos.

questions.q: What does Georgina say the 'backlash' involves?
options: Shops stopping all their online sales to save waste
People buying second-hand and mending their clothes
Governments banning very cheap clothes from abroad
People leaving social media to avoid fashion adverts
questions.why: She says some people now promise to buy second-hand, make do with what they have and mend clothes.
